context: Instacart is a grocery delivery and pickup marketplace that connects customers with personal shoppers who pick items from a partner store's inventory.
Instacart charges delivery fees plus an optional service fee, and offers an Instacart+ membership with reduced fees.
Instacart's app shows estimated item availability and allows customers to pre-approve substitutions for out-of-stock items before checkout.
assumptions: assumed: Instacart logs discrete events for store-selected, item-added-to-cart, checkout-started, fees-and-substitution-preferences-reviewed, and order-placed, tied to a session
assumed: cart abandonment is highest at the point fees and estimated total are first shown in full, based on how the checkout flow surfaces pricing
followUps: If the drop is concentrated at the fee-reveal step, how would you separate 'sticker shock at the total' from 'sticker shock specifically at the service/delivery fee line items'?
How would you test whether showing the full estimated total earlier in the flow (before cart-building) helps or hurts conversion?
A cohort of users abandons after setting substitution preferences rather than before — what would you hypothesize, and how would you check it?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the funnel is logged step by step from store selection through order placement, and that fee visibility is a likely friction point given how delivery/marketplace apps typically structure checkout. Plan: quick context on Instacart's two-sided model, walk the funnel steps, isolate the leak, propose a test-backed fix with a guardrail.

Instacart's business model depends on fees layered onto a marketplace transaction — delivery fee, service fee, and often a markup on item prices versus in-store — which makes checkout price transparency a real tension: reveal too late and you get cart abandonment, reveal too early and you may deter cart-building altogether. The company's strategic bet with Instacart+ is to convert price-sensitive high-frequency users into a flat-fee membership, so understanding whether checkout abandonment is fee-driven directly informs both funnel fixes and membership positioning.

Stepping through the funnel: store-selected to first-item-added isolates browsing friction; item-added to checkout-started isolates cart-building intent; checkout-started to fees-reviewed isolates the pricing-reveal moment; fees-reviewed to order-placed isolates final commitment. I'd expect the sharpest drop between checkout-started and order-placed, and within that step I'd split by whether the fee total shown is above or below the user's typical historical order value — a good proxy for whether this order's fees feel unusually high relative to what they're used to paying. If abandonment concentrates among users whose fee-to-subtotal ratio is unusually high for a small cart, that points to fee structure discouraging small orders specifically, not price sensitivity in general — confirmed by checking if those same users complete larger orders at a normal rate. The fix would be a minimum-cart-size nudge or a fee cap for small orders rather than a blanket fee reduction. I'd track order-placed rate for small carts as the recovery metric, guardrailed by average order value platform-wide (make sure the nudge doesn't just shrink baskets to hit a threshold) and by Instacart+ membership conversion rate among affected users (the fee-sensitive segment is exactly who membership should convert).

For the checkout/pricing team, I'd set a goal to raise order-placed rate for small-basket sessions by a defined percentage this quarter, sized against the current gap between small-cart and large-cart conversion. This is directly actionable through fee structure or threshold nudges, jointly owned with the growth team on the Instacart+ guardrail so the fix also feeds the membership funnel rather than just patching one-time orders.

pitfalls: Concluding 'fees are too high' without segmenting by cart size, missing that the issue may be fee-to-subtotal ratio on small orders specifically
Fixing checkout abandonment with a blanket fee cut that erodes margin instead of a targeted small-cart intervention

cases.title: Diagnose the signup-to-first-trade funnel for Coinbase
cases.prompt: Coinbase requires identity verification before a new user can fund an account and place their first trade. Walk me through how you'd analyze the signup-to-first-trade funnel and find where the biggest leak is.
context: Coinbase is a publicly traded cryptocurrency exchange that requires identity verification (KYC) as part of account setup, consistent with financial-services regulatory requirements.
Coinbase supports multiple funding methods, including bank transfer and debit card, which typically carry different processing times and fees.
Coinbase offers both a simpler 'buy/sell' interface and a more advanced trading interface (Coinbase Advanced Trade) aimed at different user segments.
assumptions: assumed: Coinbase logs discrete events for signup-started, identity-verification-submitted, identity-verification-approved, funding-method-added, funds-available, and first-trade-placed, tied to a user
assumed: identity verification has a meaningfully higher abandonment or delay rate than other steps, given it depends on a third-party or manual review process outside Coinbase's direct control
followUps: If identity-verification-submitted to approved has a long tail (some users waiting days), how would you distinguish a systemic review bottleneck from a small number of genuinely flagged cases?
How would you measure whether users who abandon after approval but before funding are blocked by their bank's own restrictions on crypto-related transfers, versus losing intent?
Regulatory requirements mean you can't simply remove or shorten identity verification — what levers are actually available to you here?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume each step from signup through first trade is logged, and that identity verification is a likely bottleneck given it depends on external review rather than a Coinbase-controlled UI flow. Plan: brief context on why this funnel is regulatorily constrained in ways a typical app isn't, step through it, isolate the biggest controllable leak, propose a fix with a compliance-aware guardrail.

Coinbase operates under securities and financial-services regulation, so identity verification isn't optional friction to be designed away — it's a compliance requirement, and Coinbase's business depends on maintaining that trust with regulators to keep operating. That constraint reframes the exercise: the goal isn't removing verification, it's making the parts of the funnel that ARE within Coinbase's control (funding, first-trade UX) as smooth as possible so verification isn't compounded by avoidable friction elsewhere.

Stepping through the funnel: signup-started to verification-submitted isolates whether the initial ask is clear; verification-submitted to approved isolates the (largely external) review step; approved to funding-method-added isolates whether users return promptly after approval; funding-added to funds-available isolates payment-method processing time; funds-available to first-trade isolates final execution friction. Since verification timing isn't fully controllable, I'd focus analysis on approved-to-funding-added, since a real drop there means users who cleared the hardest step still don't come back — I'd segment by time-since-approval-notification and by whether the user received a push/email at approval, since a delayed or missing notification is a plausible, fixable cause distinct from lost intent. If users notified immediately convert to funding-added at a much higher rate than users with delayed notifications, that isolates a notification-timing fix rather than a funding-UX fix. I'd track funding-added rate within 24 hours of approval as the recovery metric, guardrailed by verification approval rate itself (make sure no change pressures the compliance team to approve faster at the cost of rigor) and by first-trade completion rate among funded users (confirm the fix converts all the way through, not just to a funded-but-idle account).

For the activation/lifecycle team, I'd set a goal to raise the share of approved users who fund an account within 24 hours by a defined percentage this quarter, sized against the current same-day conversion rate. This is achievable through notification timing and reminder design without touching the verification process itself, and I'd keep the compliance team as a required reviewer on the goal so no proposed change is read as pressure to relax verification rigor.

pitfalls: Treating the identity-verification step as a normal UX problem to optimize, ignoring that it's a regulatory requirement outside product's control
Proposing a fix to verification speed that could be read as pressuring compliance to cut corners

cases.title: Diagnose the signup-to-first-order funnel for Swiggy
cases.prompt: A new Swiggy user downloads the app, browses restaurants, but a large share never place a first order. Walk me through how you'd analyze this signup-to-first-order funnel and find the leak.
context: Swiggy is a food and grocery delivery platform operating across Indian cities, with restaurant listings that vary by the user's delivery location.
Swiggy shows estimated delivery time and a delivery fee that can vary based on distance and demand at the time of ordering.
Swiggy offers a loyalty/membership program (Swiggy One) that reduces or waives delivery fees for subscribers.
assumptions: assumed: Swiggy logs discrete events for app-opened, location-set, restaurant-viewed, item-added-to-cart, checkout-started, and order-placed, tied to a user
assumed: the funnel varies meaningfully by city tier, with a lower first-order conversion rate in newly launched or lower-density service areas
followUps: If first-order conversion is meaningfully lower in newer/lower-density cities, how would you distinguish 'fewer restaurant options' from 'higher delivery fees due to distance' as the driver?
How would you check if users are comparing prices against a competing app in another tab/app before deciding, versus abandoning outright?
What early signal, before order-placed, would predict whether a new user is likely to become a repeat orderer?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the funnel from app-open through order-placed is logged per user, and that first-order conversion likely varies by city tier given how delivery marketplaces scale unevenly across geographies. Plan: context on Swiggy's location-dependent model, step through the funnel, isolate whether the leak is options, pricing, or something else, propose a fix with a guardrail.

Swiggy's marketplace is fundamentally supply-constrained by geography — restaurant selection, delivery fees, and delivery time all depend on how dense Swiggy's restaurant and rider network is in a given user's exact location, which means a first-order funnel problem in one city might be a completely different problem in another. Since customer acquisition cost is a real business cost, understanding whether new users fail to convert due to genuinely thin supply versus a fixable UX issue determines whether the fix is a product change or a supply/ops investment.

Stepping through the funnel: app-opened to location-set isolates onboarding friction; location-set to restaurant-viewed isolates whether listings load and look appealing; restaurant-viewed to cart-added isolates menu/price friction; cart-added to order-placed isolates checkout and fee friction. I'd segment every step by city tier and by restaurant count within the user's delivery radius, since a thin-supply area will show a drop specifically at restaurant-viewed to cart-added (nothing appealing to order) while a thick-supply area with a drop at cart-added to order-placed points to fee or checkout friction instead. If new-city users show a large restaurant-viewed to cart-added drop that correlates with low restaurant density in their pincode, that's a supply problem, not a product one, and no checkout redesign will fix it. I'd track first-order conversion rate segmented by restaurant-density tier as the primary metric, guardrailed by average delivery fee shown (make sure any supply-side subsidy to increase restaurant count doesn't just push up fees elsewhere) and by 30-day repeat-order rate for new converts (confirm the fix produces real customers, not one-time discount-chasers).

For the supply/expansion team in low-density cities, I'd set a goal to raise first-order conversion in the bottom restaurant-density tier by a defined percentage this quarter, tied to a specific restaurant-onboarding target for those pincodes rather than a product-only fix. Guardrails on delivery fee and repeat-order rate stay jointly owned with the pricing and retention teams so supply growth doesn't just shift the problem into a fee or quality issue.

pitfalls: Treating a low first-order conversion rate as a single problem, missing that its cause differs by city tier and restaurant density
Proposing a checkout/UX fix for what is actually a restaurant-supply gap in newer cities

cases.title: Diagnose the signup-to-first-SIP funnel for Groww
cases.prompt: Groww lets users set up a recurring Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) into mutual funds, which requires KYC and linking a bank account via mandate before the first SIP installment can be debited. Walk me through how you'd analyze the signup-to-first-SIP-installment funnel.
context: Groww is an Indian investment platform offering mutual funds, stocks, and other instruments, requiring KYC (identity verification) under Indian financial regulations before a user can invest.
Setting up a SIP requires linking a bank account and authorizing a recurring auto-debit mandate (commonly via NACH or UPI Autopay), separate from the KYC step.
Groww provides fund-comparison tools and risk-profiling questionnaires to help users select mutual funds before committing to a SIP.
assumptions: assumed: Groww logs discrete events for signup-completed, KYC-submitted, KYC-approved, fund-selected, SIP-mandate-setup-started, mandate-approved, and first-installment-debited, tied to a user

assumed: the mandate-authorization step (approving the auto-debit in a separate banking app or via OTP) has a materially lower completion rate than the in-app steps, since it requires leaving Groww's own flow
followUps: If mandate-approval has a lower completion rate for UPI Autopay versus NACH, what would that suggest, and how would you confirm it?
How would you tell apart users who never intended to complete the mandate from users who tried and had it rejected by their bank?
What would you test to improve the specific step of leaving Groww's app to approve a mandate elsewhere?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the funnel from signup through first-installment is logged per user, and that the mandate-approval step — which requires the user to leave Groww's app and confirm in their banking app or via a separate flow — is a likely leak given it's outside Groww's direct UI control. Plan: brief context on why SIP setup is a multi-hop regulated flow, step through the funnel, isolate the leak, propose a fix with a compliance-aware guardrail.

Groww's SIP product depends on two separate regulated steps — KYC and a recurring-debit mandate — that both involve leaving the core app experience at some point, which is unusual friction for a consumer app but non-negotiable under Indian financial regulation. Groww's growth strategy relies on converting India's large under-invested population into regular investors, so a leak specifically at the hand-off-to-another-app step directly limits how many first-time investors actually start investing versus merely browsing funds.

Stepping through the funnel: signup to KYC-submitted isolates the initial documentation ask; KYC-submitted to approved isolates the (partly external) verification step; KYC-approved to fund-selected isolates whether users engage with fund-selection tools; fund-selected to mandate-setup-started isolates initial SIP commitment; mandate-started to mandate-approved isolates the external hand-off; mandate-approved to first-installment-debited isolates final execution. I'd expect the sharpest drop at mandate-started to mandate-approved specifically, since it requires leaving Groww's app, and I'd segment that step by mandate type (NACH vs UPI Autopay) since they have different user flows and bank-side friction. If UPI Autopay shows meaningfully lower completion than NACH despite being the newer, supposedly-faster method, that points to a specific UX or bank-compatibility issue in that hand-off rather than mandate-setup being inherently leaky. I'd track mandate-approved rate segmented by mandate type as the recovery metric, guardrailed by KYC approval rate (confirm no upstream change is pressuring compliance) and by 3-month SIP-continuation rate (make sure a smoother mandate flow doesn't just produce first-installment conversions that lapse immediately after).

For the payments/mandate team, I'd set a goal to close the completion-rate gap between UPI Autopay and NACH mandates by a defined percentage this quarter, since that gap is the most specific and actionable signal in the funnel. I'd keep KYC-approval rate and 3-month SIP-continuation as guardrails jointly owned with compliance and retention so the fix doesn't trade one problem for another.

pitfalls: Treating the mandate-approval hand-off as unfixable because it happens outside the app, missing that mandate-type UX still varies and is addressable
Optimizing for first-installment conversion without checking that those installments continue past month one

cases.title: Diagnose the free-to-Super trial conversion funnel for Duolingo
cases.prompt: Duolingo offers a free trial of its ad-free, unlimited-hearts Super subscription, often triggered by hitting the daily lesson-mistake limit on the free tier. Walk me through how you'd analyze the trial-start-to-paid-conversion funnel.
context: Duolingo is a language-learning app with a free ad-supported tier and a paid Super subscription that removes ads and the 'hearts' mistake-limit mechanic.
Duolingo commonly prompts free users to start a Super trial at moments of friction, such as running out of hearts mid-lesson.
Duolingo's free tier limits how many mistakes a user can make before being blocked from further lessons until hearts refill or are purchased/earned.
assumptions: assumed: Duolingo logs discrete events for trial-started, trial-day-1-session, trial-mid-trial-session, trial-ended, and paid-conversion, tied to a user
assumed: trial-starters who hit the hearts limit as their trigger convert to paid at a different rate than trial-starters who opted in proactively from a settings/upsell screen
followUps: If hearts-limit-triggered trials convert lower than proactive trials, does that mean the trigger is a worse acquisition channel, or that it's reaching a less-committed segment that would churn regardless of trial design?
How would you test whether reminding users of remaining trial days affects conversion, without the reminder itself feeling like nagging?
What early-trial behavior (in the first 2-3 days) would you use as a leading indicator of eventual conversion?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume each trial-lifecycle event is logged with the trigger type (hearts-limit vs proactive opt-in), since that distinction seems central to interpreting conversion differences. Plan: brief context on why the trigger matters for Duolingo's model, step through the trial funnel, isolate where and for whom it leaks, propose a fix with a guardrail against manipulative framing.

Duolingo's core free experience is built around light friction (the hearts mechanic) that's meant to nudge engagement and, incidentally, create natural moments to introduce Super — but the company's stated brand identity leans on being encouraging rather than punitive, so a trial funnel fix that leans too hard on frustration-driven upsells risks working against that brand positioning even if it lifts short-term conversion.

Stepping through the funnel: trial-started to day-1-session isolates immediate engagement; day-1 to mid-trial-session isolates sustained usage; mid-trial to trial-ended isolates whether the trial period itself is used fully; trial-ended to paid-conversion isolates the final decision. I'd segment every step by trigger type (hearts-limit vs proactive), since I'd expect proactive trial-starters to have higher intrinsic motivation and convert better regardless of trial experience, while hearts-limit-triggered users are more likely to be reacting to momentary frustration. If hearts-limit trials show lower day-1-session engagement specifically (not just lower eventual conversion), that suggests the trigger itself produces a less-engaged trial cohort from the start, not just a harder final decision — meaning the fix is in what happens right after trial-start (a clearer explanation of what Super removes), not in the final upsell screen. I'd track day-1 and day-3 trial engagement rate segmented by trigger as the leading metric, guardrailed by trial-to-annoyance signals like app-uninstall-during-trial rate (make sure the trigger itself isn't driving people away entirely) and by long-term (6-month) retention of converted subscribers by trigger type (confirm hearts-limit conversions aren't lower-quality, high-churn subscribers).

For the monetization team, I'd set a goal to raise day-3 trial engagement specifically for hearts-limit-triggered trials by a defined percentage this quarter, since that's the earliest and most diagnostic point in the gap between trigger types. I'd keep uninstall-during-trial rate and 6-month subscriber retention as guardrails jointly owned with the core-engagement and retention teams, given the brand risk of a trigger that reads as punitive rather than encouraging.

pitfalls: Treating hearts-limit-triggered trials as simply 'worse' without checking whether the issue is trial-experience design or a genuinely less-committed acquisition source
Optimizing the trial funnel toward short-term conversion in a way that risks Duolingo's encouraging brand positioning

cases.title: Diagnose the search-to-booking funnel for MakeMyTrip flights
cases.prompt: A user searches for a flight on MakeMyTrip, sees a results list, but a large share never complete a booking. Walk me through how you'd analyze the search-to-booking funnel and find the leak.
context: MakeMyTrip is an Indian online travel platform offering flight, hotel, and train bookings, aggregating fares from multiple airlines for a given route and date.
MakeMyTrip's flight search results commonly show filters for price, duration, number of stops, and airline, along with fare-type options (e.g., refundable vs non-refundable).
MakeMyTrip offers a loyalty program (MyPartner/MyBiz for business travel, and a general loyalty program for consumers) and travel insurance add-ons at checkout.
assumptions: assumed: MakeMyTrip logs discrete events for search-submitted, results-viewed, flight-selected, passenger-details-entered, add-ons-reviewed, and payment-completed, tied to a session

assumed: a meaningful share of searches are comparison-shopping (the same route/date searched across multiple travel sites in parallel) rather than single-platform intent, based on how price-comparison behavior typically works in this category
followUps: If flight-selected to passenger-details-entered has the sharpest drop, how would you distinguish 'price went up between search and selection' from users simply comparison-shopping elsewhere?
How would you test whether showing fewer, more curated results (versus a long sortable list) changes selection and completion rates?
Add-ons like travel insurance are reviewed at checkout — how would you check if they're perceived as helpful or as unwanted checkout friction?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the funnel from search through payment is logged per session, and that a meaningful share of traffic is comparison-shopping across multiple travel sites rather than committed single-platform intent, which matters for interpreting any drop-off as fixable versus inherent to the category. Plan: brief context on why travel booking funnels have unusually high comparison-shopping noise, step through the funnel, isolate the leak, propose a fix with a guardrail.

MakeMyTrip aggregates fares across airlines rather than selling its own inventory, so its core value proposition is comparison and convenience, not price control — meaning some 'abandonment' is actually users successfully using MakeMyTrip to find the best option and then booking directly or on a competitor, which the product can influence through UX and trust but can't fully eliminate. That distinction matters because a fix aimed at the wrong cause (assuming pure UX friction when it's actually competitive price-shopping) would waste effort.

Stepping through the funnel: search-submitted to results-viewed isolates whether results load reliably; results-viewed to flight-selected isolates whether the list is navigable and a choice gets made; flight-selected to passenger-details isolates fare-lock friction (a price or availability change between selection and entry); passenger-details to payment-completed isolates final checkout friction including add-ons. I'd expect the most diagnostic drop to be flight-selected to passenger-details, and within that I'd check the rate of price-change-between-selection-and-entry, since airline fares can shift in real time — if a large share of that drop coincides with a shown price increase, that's a fare-volatility problem, not a UX problem, and no checkout redesign fixes it. If instead the drop happens with no price change shown, that points to genuine checkout-entry friction (e.g., mandatory fields, unclear add-on framing) worth fixing directly. I'd track passenger-details-to-payment completion rate, segmented by whether a price change occurred, as the primary diagnostic split, guardrailed by average add-on attach rate (make sure any checkout simplification doesn't just strip out legitimately useful options) and by post-booking cancellation rate (confirm faster checkout isn't producing more mistaken bookings).

For the checkout team, I'd set a goal to raise passenger-details-to-payment completion specifically for sessions with no price change by a defined percentage this quarter, since that isolates the genuinely fixable portion of the drop from fare-volatility noise. Add-on attach rate and post-booking cancellation stay as guardrails jointly owned with the monetization and customer-experience teams so a faster checkout doesn't trade completion for downstream quality.

pitfalls: Treating every unit of search-to-booking drop-off as a fixable UX problem, ignoring that comparison-shopping across travel sites is inherent to the category
Simplifying checkout by stripping add-ons without checking their attach rate or usefulness first
